source_metadata.title: MAP-Graph: Provenance-Aware Shared Memory for Multi-Agent Workflows
source_metadata.source_type: arXiv preprint / AI multi-agent systems benchmark and architecture paper

atoms.canonical_statement: The evaluation asks whether MAP-Graph improves utility, prevents poisoned/private/revoked memory from crossing read or action boundaries, and preserves those effects across domains, scenarios, and model backbones.
MAP-Graph is implemented as a task-scoped memory backend that couples a NetworkX MultiDiGraph with an ephemeral Chroma collection through shared memory identifiers and resets both between tasks.

The provenance graph uses eight registered node types (User, Agent, Tool, Resource, Message, Memory, Claim, Action) and ten registered edge types for authorization, observation, forwarding, derivation, summarization, writing, reading, verification, invalidation, and action use.
Graph construction uses observable workflow state and task-provided metadata and does not require private chain-of-thought.

A derived memory inherits the intersection of referenced permission scopes; if no referenced scope exists all task agents are eligible, and if the intersection is empty access falls back to the writing agent.
Retrieval first removes permission-ineligible records with CanRead and only then ranks eligible records, preventing semantic similarity from overriding a detected access restriction.

For eligible memories, MAP-Graph multiplies semantic similarity by clipped path trust; path trust is the product of source trust, path integrity, transformation factor, permission validity, verification bonus, and writer reliability, and the top five scores are returned.

At action time MAP-Graph uses risk-indexed thresholds of 0.30 for answer actions, 0.60 for low/medium-risk non-answer actions, and 0.85 for high-risk non-answer actions, with ordered rules that can return Block, Reverify, AskUser, Redact, or Allow.
Affected descendants are retained and marked rather than deleted, so containment restricts retrieval or action use while preserving lineage for audit.

The full benchmark contains 2,700 synthetic tasks generated with seed 42, evenly spanning corporate workflow, software engineering, and research assistance and six experiment groups; oracle labels are 960 Allow, 1,140 Block, 210 Reverify, and 390 Redact.

The main comparison evaluates seven baselines plus MAP-Graph on the same 2,700 tasks, six ablations on the same task set, and selected methods across three generation backbones on a fixed stratified 540-task subset.

Before execution, the runtime sanitizer removes oracle decisions, evaluator rationales, experiment/family/variant identifiers, and should_be_used annotations while retaining provenance, visibility, ownership, trust, risk, permission fields, and authorized source text.

Main experiments use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at temperature 0 with one four-role round, at most five retrieved memories, and normalized BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings with k=5 for embedding-based methods.
Reported 95% intervals use 2,000 cluster-bootstrap samples over semantic families and quantify within-run case-family variation rather than model-inference nondeterminism.
MAP-Graph achieved 94.96% task success rate (TSR), compared with 74.67% for B6 Flat Provenance, the strongest TSR baseline.

atoms.canonical_statement: The benchmark is synthetic and templated, actions are simulated, and each task uses only one four-agent round.
A single temperature-zero run does not estimate inference nondeterminism, and a nontrivial fraction of outer calls reached the 2,048-token cap.
TSR can credit a safe but non-exact intervention, so it must be interpreted together with exact decision accuracy.
B3 through B5 are benchmark adaptations of prior systems rather than complete reproductions.
Latency is not reported as a paper-facing metric because experiments used concurrent remote shared endpoints, preventing separation of provider queuing from local memory overhead.
MAP-Graph does not implement a generic supersession or contradiction state machine and does not claim automatic open-domain conflict resolution or a universal notion of truth.

Within the controlled benchmark, the authors conclude that provenance can be used as an operational control for retrieval and actions rather than only as post-hoc audit metadata, while calling for repeated, less templated, cross-session, and deployment-scale testing.
